newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: MOTOR RACING-HILL SCRAPES ONTO GRID AS VILLENEUVE RULES.
newsitem.headline: MOTOR RACING-HILL SCRAPES ONTO GRID AS VILLENEUVE RULES.

text.p: World drivers champion Damon Hill suffered a humiliating start to his title defence on Saturday when he scraped into the season-opening Australian Grand Prix on the back row of the grid.
The 36-year-Briton, unceremoniously discarded by the Williams team mid-way through last season, was beset with gearbox problems in his first competitive outing with his new Arrows team.

While Hill struggled, Canadian Jacques Villeneuve, the driver who assumed the mantle of Williams number one driver, established his credentials as championship favourite by recording a time almost two seconds faster than the field in a stunning display.
Villeneuve, 25, who finished runner-up to Hill in 1996, smashed the qualifying lap record by almost three seconds to grab pole position for Sunday's race at Albert Park.

In contrast, Hill looked likely to miss out on qualifying for all but the final minutes of the session, securing 20th place on the grid with his penultimate timed lap. Asked how he felt about his performance in a car carrying the world champion's number one, Hill said: "I feel it is more disappointing than embarrassing.

"I feel I am a front row driver and I feel a bit uncomfortable about being on the back row on the grid," said Hill, whose team-mate Pedro Diniz of Brazil was one of three drivers who failed to qualify.
Villeneuve was understandably delighted about his qualifying time of one minute 29.369 seconds as he seeks his fifth win in 17 grand prix starts.
"There is a big gap between myself and my team-mate (Heinz-Harald Frentzen) and the rest of grid. It is very satisfying for me," said Villeneuve, a former IndyCar champion.
German Frentzen, who switched from Sauber to replace Hill, was second fastest in a time almost two seconds slower than Villeneuve.
In his media conference later, Villeneuve added a word of sympathy for Hill's predicament.
"He was my team-mate and he is the champion. He is not one of those guys who are five laps behind everyone else all the time and should not be there.
"It is difficult for me to see him back there," Villeneuve said.
Double world champion Michael Schumacher of Germany was third fastest in his Ferrari in a time of one minute 31.472s.

"Looking at the gap between the two Williams, almost two seconds, I expect Villeneuve to disappear into the distance tomorrow (Sunday) and I will be fighting for a place on the podium," Schumacher said.
"I am quite happy -- third place is a little bit better than I expected," who joined Villeneuve in expressing sympathy for Hill's plight.
With two drivers on the front row, Williams maintained the superiority that gave them the constructors' title last year.
Frentzen claimed his place with a fast lap only seconds before the end of the qualifying session, proving he has what is need to be a replacement for Hill.
"For me, it's the best qualification so far in my career in Formula One, so I'm happy now.
Villeneuve claimed pole position on his debut with Williams in Melbourne last year, while Hill went on to win the race, creating the launch pad for his first world championship success.
Apart from Villeneuve's utter dominance, the rest of the field were locked in a highly-competitive session on a mild and cloudy Melbourne afternoon.
Behind Frentzen, the Ferraris and McLarens were in close competition, with Schumacher and his British team-mate Eddie Irvine edging narrowly ahead of Briton David Coulthard and Finn Mika Hakkinen.
